articles.content: US ports face onslaught of cyber attacks by Mira Bhakta - 11/22/26 1:05 PM ET Link copied - 11/22/26 1:05 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure.  The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.’s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with “hundreds if not thousands” of attacks per day, according to reporting from the Financial Times .  The port’s chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from “known bad actor” countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets.  The attacks against Corpus Christi’s port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per the Financial Times.  “They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.” He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but “if you’re playing defence, you have to get it right every time … if you’re planning offence, you only have to get it right once.” The Port of Los Angeles — the country’s busiest port — similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported .  Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, expressed that all potential attackers “have to do is to get it right one time” and that it was “front of mind every day.” The port’s cybersecurity operations team has scaled up in recent years, now forming a seven-layer digital defense, he added, per Bloomberg. This comes after the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Department of Homeland Security launched a hub to fight cyber criminals — connecting more than 30 federal agencies with hundreds of state and local partners. “It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible,” the DOJ said in a statement. “It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support.” The Port of Corpus Christi didn’t respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment. articles.title: Ukrainian Maritime Drones Sink Russian Warship at Libyan Port
articles.content: Satellite image shows the capsized Russian navy corvette, the Merkury, after a suspected drone strike at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya. Photograph: 2026 Vantor/AP View image in fullscreen Satellite image shows the capsized Russian navy corvette, the Merkury, after a suspected drone strike at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya. Photograph: 2026 Vantor/AP Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government. Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press. View image in fullscreen Aerial view of the Russian naval vessel Merkury before it was struck in the port of Benghazi, Libya, 21 November 2026. Photograph: 2026 Vantor/EPA Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine , marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war. Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe. Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion. Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known. Map showing location of Benghazi, Libya Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia. There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines. The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X. The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured. It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible. “The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said. 0:55 Large blaze at Benghazi port after suspected drone attack on Russian warship – video The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed. HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship. View image in fullscreen An explosion on the ship in Benghazi, where it had been refuelling on its way back to Russia. Photograph: X.com If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war. But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port. A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year. Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria. Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze. View image in fullscreen Emergency services working to extinguish a fire onboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was struck in the Baltic Sea on Saturday. Photograph: Finnish Border Guard/Reuters The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured. On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said. The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory. The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday. Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. articles.title: OpenAI Chief Scientist Calls for Mandatory Compute Caps
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Nov 23, 2026, 06:40 AM Updated Nov 23, 2026, 06:40 AM Set as preferred source Summarise OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki urged industrywide limits on AI development until researchers can better understand and monitor advanced models. He proposed common thresholds, possibly using “perplexity”, and warned AI could speed up its own progress by 2027, outpacing safety oversight. Sam Altman backed the idea, while the US prepares for tougher AI regulation debates and possible clashes with President Donald Trump over restrictions. AI generated SAN FRANCISCO, California – OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behaviour. Jakub Pachocki called for industrywide standards that would establish thresholds for AI development, with companies agreeing not to exceed them until specific safety requirements are met, according to a post published on Nov 22. “I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behaviour achieves a certain concrete milestone,” Pachocki wrote. The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. Pachocki did not specify what the initial limit should be or when it might take effect. Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate advances in its own development as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing improvements in researchers’ ability to monitor and understand the technology. OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile”. He said in a post on social media platform X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control”. The proposal comes as the US prepares for renewed debate over AI regulation following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections. The party’s gains in the House, Senate and governors’ races could bring greater congressional scrutiny of technology companies and renewed efforts to establish AI safety rules. Some lawmakers are also discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to coordinate AI policy. US President Donald Trump has opposed broad restrictions on AI development, setting up a potential clash with the incoming Democratic Congress over how to regulate the technology. articles.content: Agence France-Presse Nov 22, 2026 Add AL-MONITOR on Google A Sudanese man stands on the rubble of a destroyed building following a drone strike on a neighbourhood of Khartoum — Ebrahim HAMID Drones struck Sudan's capital Khartoum, damaging residential homes and a United Nations building on Sunday, witnesses and the world organisation said. Explosions were heard in the area around Khartoum airport and other parts of the city from around 2:00 am until approximately 4:30 am. A drone strike completely destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia. "The drone attack at dawn today is a continuation of Ethiopian aggression against Sudanese territory, as the drones were launched from Ethiopia's Bahir Dar airport," the source told AFP. Sudan's military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), against which it has been fighting since April 2023, including through drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia denies the accusations. AFP footage showed a house reduced to rubble, with a security perimeter around the site. Pieces of furniture, household items and clothing were scattered among the debris. Al-Nour Adam, who lives in the area, told AFP that upon entering the house after the strike, "we found a person lying on a bed, wounded in his left arm, chest and head". - 'Where are we supposed to go?' - "The strikes are indiscriminate," Adam said. "A strike could hit while you are asleep. You might wake up to find your children gone... It is truly tragic. You cannot be certain of anything." Yasser Hassan, another resident, said that the occupants of the house "had only just moved in, after searching for shelter for a long time".  "Then the drone struck them. Where are we supposed to go?" Another witness reported that a drone hit the home of a mosque's muezzin, the person who calls Muslims to prayer, in Jebel Aulia, around 45 kilometres (28 miles) south of Khartoum. "People were trying to rescue family members trapped under the rubble," the witness said. The United Nations, meanwhile, said that "a UN premises with UN colleagues in the building was damaged". "This occurred in a civilian neighbourhood," the UN's humanitarian office (OCHA) said in a statement posted on X. OCHA condemned the risk posed to humanitarian workers, saying it was "unacceptable" that UN personnel were being exposed to such danger. Saudi Arabia, which has provided support to the Sudanese regular army in the country's war, said on X that it "categorically rejects these brutal attacks". - Drone warfare - Authorities did not immediately report on casualties. The conflict between the RSF and the Sudanese army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises. The United Nations has repeatedly criticised both sides' rampant use of drones, which killed more than 1,100 people in the first half of 2026. Of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes, the UN said. A Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village days ago, as the army pushed through the state, recapturing territory from the RSF. The rival forces have for the last year wrestled for control of the resource-rich southern Kordofan region, which connects the army-held centre and east to RSF-controlled Darfur. In recent months, both the army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometres away without risking their fighters. str-stm/amj/rh This one's on us. articles.title: Goldman Sachs Warns AI Capex Unwind Threatens Structural Markets
articles.content: The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year . Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom. Recommended Video Snider’s note said the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days. Goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged. Goldman said any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning. Condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40 times trailing sales for Anthropic. A US Bank Asset Management executive said the valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” Goldman’s own outlook says the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond “is highly uncertain.” Condition 2: the Fed. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, and the Fed meets Dec. 9. Goldman’s economists expect hikes in December and March, sending the federal funds rate to a peak of 4.25% to 4.5%. A dovish signal looks unlikely soon. Treasuries did rally sharply Friday as investors looked for safety, which is not the same as a Fed pivot. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%. Condition 3: A big drop in investor positioning. This has often marked the end of past drawdowns. The first condition is unsettled, to say the least. Anthropic’s historic IPO turned into a sort of referendum on the entire AI trade, an unfair weight to put on a single, albeit remarkably important, company. The company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, passing SpaceX’s $85.7 billion as the biggest IPO on record. The shares jumped 17% on Thursday, then gave most of it back Friday to close at $88.91 , not far above the $83 IPO price. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly,” said Dakota Wealth’s Robert Pavlik. “I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company… I think they’re just skeptical of this market.” Morgan Stanley , the underwriter tasked with stabilizing the shares, closed its support position , removing a potential pillar of support. UBS said the debate had shifted from whether AI investment will continue to whether it can generate enough revenue and returns for shareholders. A Capital Economics economist wrote that the IPO’s success while other AI stocks fell shows the parts of the AI ecosystem “no longer move as one,” as chipmakers Nvidia , Broadcom , Micron and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14% . Nvidia’s 14% fall on Friday was its worst day in almost two years. It lost 22.9% on the week and is down 47.5% since Oct. 6, a loss of $2.7 trillion in market value. Reuters reported the SEC is probing its accounting practices . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 , and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The VIX, Wall Street’s “Fear Gauge,” closed at 35.89, its highest in 19 months . “It’s a meltdown right now,” said Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research. JPMorgan Asset Management’s David Kelly took the other view: “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu.” On the third condition, Goldman’s note says hedge funds have already cut back. Their net leverage is the lowest since April 2025. A companion report, Snider’s Hedge Fund Trend Monitor, says the most popular hedge fund longs were crowded into the AI trade and have lagged the S&P 500 by 14 percentage points over six months. That is among the worst stretches in the basket’s 20-year history. The note described the situation for hedge funds as “bruised and broadening.” But Goldman’s broader Sentiment Indicator is still above average. U.S. equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in nearly $170 billion in the fourth quarter so far. Asset managers’ net equity futures positions are in the 82nd percentile of the past 10 years. Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. Goldman Research says AI capital spending produced “about half” of this year’s earnings growth. The Street is split on whether this is the top. Capital Economics expects further declines. Goldman’s Nov. 17 outlook , written before the drop, forecast 8,700 by the end of 2027. In the Nov. 20 note, its range runs from about 5,800 to 8,100 depending on whether investors regain confidence in earnings. From Friday’s close, that is roughly 16% downside and 17% upside. Those percentages are my math, not Goldman’s. After the 22 S&P 500 corrections since 1980, the index averaged a 4% return over the next three months. It rose in 17 of them. E*Trade’s research is less reassuring. Of the 14 times since 1983, the index first closed 10% or more below a record, five became bear markets. articles.title: One Dollar of GPT Tokens Defeats Chinese Firewall
articles.content: asia in brief PLUS: Lenovo's infra group finally makes big profit; Indonesia’s glaciers are gone; Australian bank releases its AI bug-finder; and more! Simon Sharwood Simon Sharwood Asia-Pacific Editor Published mon 23 Nov 2026 // 00:23 UTC Make us preferred on Google Come for the science, stay for the big iron: Supercomputer admin on why he loves the job 16 hours ago ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo 1 day ago Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans 2 days ago China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server 2 days ago Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses 2 days ago Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens. That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control. Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI. The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.” “CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.” The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1. The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar. “CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.” Lenovo finally cracks monster datacenter profits Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers. The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit. In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the company revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo says it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share. Lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The company claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter. Indonesia’s glaciers are all but gone It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form. Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S.  Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice. NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that shows most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently showed just .09km 2 of ice remained.  “To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.” For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” –  the highest point on each continent. The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees . The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu. Australian bank giving away its bug-hunter Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.” The bank says analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.” The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub , where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code. Japan’s space program hands some launches to Mitsubishi Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running launches of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations. The deal means MHI will handle launches for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters. JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations. Once JAXA is satisfied those new rigs are reliable, it plans to transition them to private operators, too. ®   china censorship australia ai and ml great firewall security jaxa lenovo indonesia Make us preferred on Google

articles.content: Kit piggybacks off TV and mobile signals and can be neatly stuffed into an SUV Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published sun 22 Nov 2026 // 09:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare 9 days ago Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss 10 days ago Royal Navy stands up first autonomous boat squadron 12 days ago Ericsson says it can detect, track drones using only mobile networks 20 days ago Attack on BAE-managed system disrupts US bankruptcy courts October 16, 2026 BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position. The defense biz says its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal. Conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies. Passive radar is not new, but BAE says its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," says BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd. The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says. (Representational image) Mumbai: In its first advisory, the newly-formed self-regulatory body (SRB) last week urged all crypto platforms and intermediaries to review their products, transaction flows, and overseas or group-entity arrangements to be on the right side of laws on foreign exchange, payments, tax, and anti-money laundering . The Enforcement Directorate 's (ED's) action, said the cautionary message, has raised serious allegations of cross-border transactions using virtual digital assets (VDAs). Shortly before the advisory, the industry began lobbying with New Delhi to find a corner for cryptos in Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) -- the statute that it is beginning to trip over. In early November, two Indian exchanges -- CoinDcX , a large platform -- and Delta were searched by ED for alleged unauthorised cross-border deals involving crypto derivatives . Under the circumstances, the SRB is nudging members to seek independent legal advice in completing the legal and operational review in 60 days, a person familiar with the communique told ET. The SRB advisory, sent to the industry body which would share it with member platforms, has also warned that certain advertisements, particularly on crypto derivatives, may contravene the industry guidelines as well as amount to unfair trade practices or misleading advertisement under Consumer Protection Act , 2019. Crypto operations often come across as sharp transactions as local exchanges freely deal with overseas exchanges in sourcing liquidity to close trades. Since cryptos are not mined in India and the market here is shallow, counterparty trades to match the buyer or seller from India are often sourced from abroad. Sometimes exchanges directly import cryptos or purchase from Indian liquidity providers. Such fund transfers for crypto import/export, irrespective of who does then, are disapproved in normal course by banks handling forex remittance. Live Events According to Purushottam Anand, partner, Solvo Legal, "FEMA does not specify whether crypto is to be treated as foreign exchange, foreign security, asset outside India, or another category or instrument. Recent enforcement actions have cast legal uncertainty over most cross-border VDA transactions which are critical to sourcing liquidity and the sector's survival." A targeted amendment that clarifies the characterisation of VDAs under FEMA and creates a reportable route for Indian crypto entities is essential, said Anand who advises several crypto firms. Any such amendment must apply prospectively, he said. If cryptocurrencies were to be formally classified as 'currency' under FEMA, an interesting key question would be who would act as gatekeeper for cross-border crypto transfers -- the authorised dealer banks or FIU-registered crypto exchanges, or a combination of the two, asks Harshal Bhuta, co-founder of Ascentium India, a Singapore-headquartered professional services firm. Any such framework would have to allocate responsibility for verifying purpose of transfers, applying relevant limits, and ensuring reporting compliance, said Bhuta. The industry too wants the government to introduce FEMA rules to allow crypto sourcing from abroad - transactions which's at the core of platforms and on which is now under ED's scrutiny. The SRB is not a government recognised self-regulatory organisation. Still, it has strongly advised platforms to review existing advertising and promotional material, and immediately withdraw anything that fails to comply. articles.title: Cash Crisis Crushes Trump-Backed Industrial Robotics Venture
articles.content: LivestreamMenuFoundation employees were told their health coverage had been terminated retroactively to October, per a memo obtained by CNBC. Healthcare administrator Rippling told CNBC that Foundation had struggled to meet payroll and benefits obligations for months.Foundation is pursuing an emergency bridge loan and has been in talks with venture capital firms as it waits for a potential $150 million investment from South Korea's Base Group, which has business ties to the Trump Organization.Foundation Future Industries, a start-up founded in 2024, aims to leverage humanoid robots for military and industrial work, rather than household tasks and the service sector.Foundation Future IndustriesEmployees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump. Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket. "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November." Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month. A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment. In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider. But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said. In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated." Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment. The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said. Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized. Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said. The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added. Sign In What's Included Exclusive Stories Daily ePaper Access Smart Market Tools Curated Investment Ideas Ad-lite Experience Subscription Agencies Anouska Ladds, Executive VP, Asia Pacific Image courtesy: Mastercard Mastercard is doubling down on India's commercial payments business, Anouska Ladds , executive VP, commercial & new payment flows, Asia Pacific, tells ET in Singapore. The company is expanding engagement with banks, SMEs and large corporates, as it seeks a bigger share of the country's growing B2B payments market. Edited excerpts: What are the drivers behind this business transition? Our Mastercard strategy has three pillars: the consumer segment, our core business; services, including platforms, advisory, cyber and loyalty; and commercial and new payment flows (CNPF). We have operated in the commercial business for years, but now see a clear opportunity to support businesses of all sizes, from SMEs to large corporations, with their payment needs and beyond. This focus was put in place around two-and-a-half years ago. SMEs are the lifeblood of the economy, accounting for around 97% of businesses across Asia and driving employment and GDP. What has changed in Mastercard's approach to the B2B business? When we formally established CNPF two-and-a-half years ago, we put in place a dedicated structure, with global, regional and market leads. I have a team based in India working directly with account teams and banks. The B2B business itself didn't start two-and-a-half years ago. We had already been operating in this space and had SME and large corporate products for a long time. What is different now is the focus, dedicated resources and investment behind the business. We are gaining momentum and see this as a very strong growth area for Mastercard. Live Events How do you see the opportunity in commercial and B2B payments in India? India is an extremely exciting market. We are seeing partner banks recognise a significant opportunity, particularly in B2B payments across SMEs and large corporates. India is gaining momentum in how we service and support this segment, with banks launching new products and solutions. What makes India especially exciting is the innovation, scale of the market and opportunity to help SMEs prosper. There is significant opportunity even at the larger corporate end. India is really starting to gain momentum in how we service and support this segment. India is a critical market for us, both within the region and globally. Given the potential and runway ahead, we are only just getting started. For consumer cards, Mastercard has traditionally partnered mostly with private sector banks . Is the same approach being followed in the commercial space? Across India, we are engaging with all banks because we believe all banks have a role to play in supporting SMEs. We engage across the board and with the broader ecosystem. Banks are critical from an issuance perspective, but we are equally focused on the acceptance ecosystem. We have dedicated acceptance teams identifying key areas and segments where we need to engage merchants and businesses and demonstrate the value of card acceptance. Acceptance is a major area of focus to ensure both sides of the ecosystem develop together. What are the key payment challenges you are seeing among corporates? We have teams that work directly with corporates to understand their needs, which we call direct-to-corporate. We engage with corporates to understand their pain points, challenges and how they operate. Where there is not a card solution in place today, we look at how we can help address that. Our research shows the themes are often similar regardless of company size: friction, ease of running a business and reconciliation. For large corporates, the challenges are much bigger and more complex, with multiple systems, suppliers, reconciliation processes and large ERP environments. The challenges are larger, but the need to solve them remains the same. A lot of the talent we are hiring comes directly from corporates and ecosystem players because they deeply understand how the B2B environment operates. Have geopolitical disruptions affected the pace of your business expansion? No. We are operating in a complex geopolitical environment, not just across Asia but globally. But in the B2B world, businesses are increasingly looking for efficiency. Whether it is AI, agentic AI or broader technology trends, businesses are looking for ways to manage their operations more effectively. That is where cards, payments and related solutions can play an important role. Businesses, particularly SMEs, are managing multiple platforms and systems, so bringing them together and reducing complexity is increasingly important. We haven't seen geopolitical developments dampen demand. There may be impacts in areas such as travel and tourism spending, but we often see demand redirected elsewhere. articles.title: Anthropic Public Listing Collides With Historic Tech Selloff
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAnthropic held its historic Nasdaq debut on Thursday, raising $93.5 billion and becoming one of the most valuable companies on the planet.A day after the Claude creator started trading, Nvidia's stock closed out its longest weekly losing streak since 2008.Anthropic opened at $111.50 on Thursday and closed on Friday at $88.91.In this article Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar. "This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem. It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge, which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020. Anthropic's stock chartInvestors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence. That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX. With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits. After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025. Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar. "There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said. Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus. For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said. Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to." "At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that." Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation." That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic missed its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money." Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to use alternatives from Amazon and Google as well. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier. "It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics showed it was "going to be a very high-quality business." Anthropic isn't the only big win for VCs this year. Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz. SpaceX and Anthropic alone will make 2026 a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other year in IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering. IVP's Dash said that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027. Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the company already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board. In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would push Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range. Narasin said he wasn't even sure the company would get that far. "I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin said. That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering. "This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin said. "There was a company that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history." articles.title: Hong Kong Megaproject Displaces Traditional Industry for Tech
articles.content: Shopping trolleys were filled with dark soy sauce, black vinegar, and sweet soybean paste, all proudly touted as locally made, while workers carted in what remained of the brewer’s stock through the back and customers exchanged friendly words with grey-haired shopkeepers. Following the eviction and clearance of Kui Lee Sauce and Preserved Fruit’s factory site in Hong Kong’s northern New Territories, the 90-year-old saucemaker is counting down the days until it sells off its remaining inventory and closes its Causeway Bay storefront for good. Its now-shuttered factory was in Kwu Tung, a rural area in the New Territories tapped for development under the Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to modernise Hong Kong’s rustic frontier and deepen its integration with mainland China. The closure of the factory, opened in 1936, brings the saucemaker’s “Made in Hong Kong” legacy to an end. For Joanne Chan, a loyal customer who came by the shop to stock up on sauces ahead of its closure, the brewer’s end is emblematic of the development project’s toll, from the displacement of villagers to doubts over the demand for a new tech hub. “These traditional brands have operated for decades, but the government has no plan to let them keep going. Instead, they’re being forced to close,” she said. The factory, now sealed off after an eviction operation last month, falls within the Kwu Tung North New Development Area, which spans 447 hectares and will make way for both public and private residential developments, as well as commercial facilities and a new MTR station. The saucemaker’s factory was just a 15-minute drive from the closest border control point between Hong Kong and the neighbouring Chinese city of Shenzhen. The entire Northern Metropolis project is meant to draw Hong Kong closer to the mainland, transforming about 300 square kilometres — roughly a third of the city’s land — into an innovation and technology hub. Kui Lee’s nine decades in business have spanned three generations of the Chan family, who opened their first brewing yard in the 1940s in Kowloon City, then a hub for local brewers. Urban redevelopment in the 1960s forced Kui Lee, along with other condiment makers, into the New Territories, where the brewer remained until last month’s eviction. The rural surroundings proved to be a boon for condiment makers, as the large swathes of land allowed them to keep using traditional open-air methods to ferment and oxidise soybeans under sunlight. But most of the sauce factories that moved from Hong Kong’s urban core to its northern hinterland in the mid-20th century are now facing eviction for the Northern Metropolis. One saucemaker, Koon Chun, is fortunate enough to continue operating after the megaproject clears out its current site. Moving to its new facility, however, will take about a decade. Yuet Wo Soy Sauce, Kui Lee’s neighbour in Kwu Tung, is looking for a new site in a Tsuen Wan industrial building to stay in business. Rural villages, sawmills, and carp farms are also on their way out — with some already evicted — as deadlines loom for the Northern Metropolis project. With the October clearance operation, the family also moved out of their homes on the Kwu Tung site, according to a South China Morning Post report, which noted that power was cut off and water pipes were severed two days ahead of the clearance deadline. Joanne Chan spoke of her own experience of being evicted from a village house in Tuen Mun some two decades ago to make way for a railway line. “I understand the pain that land resumption and eviction causes; I’m strongly opposed to it,” she said. “You could grow your own fruit trees in your own yard, but after the eviction, all you get is a few hundred square feet,” she said, referring to government resettlement policies. “Those university towns and tech parks aren’t what we need as ordinary citizens.” “Go ahead, ask her,” she said, pointing to another middle-aged customer browsing the store’s wares. “Do you think she wants [artificial intelligence]?” Other customers also lamented the store’s impending closure, including a new mother buying ingredients for pork knuckle and ginger stew, a traditional postpartum dish made with sweetened black vinegar. “I don’t know where I’m going to find soy sauce when they close, especially dark soy sauce,” said another customer, Tsang, who works nearby. The condiment – darker and less salty than its counterparts and mainly used to give dishes a deeper colour – is among Kui Lee’s most well-known products. “Shops like these are getting harder to come by these days. Once one of them closes, there won’t be another to take its place. Of course, it’s a pity, but in this day and age, there’s nothing that can be done,” she said. Lawmakers warn that piping foreign state editorial narratives directly into algorithmic summaries Launders geopolitical propaganda into authoritative search results. The controversy highlights how algorithmic consolidation of news distribution transforms foundation models into ideological vectors that bypass traditional editorial accountability.

articles.title: Israeli Border Blockade Traps Thousands of Modular Gaza Shelters
articles.content: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Israel is blocking thousands of container homes destined for Gaza, adding that Israeli authorities argue Hamas could use the metal structures  for manufacturing weapons. Fidan told Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had ordered the temporary housing units, which Turkey used during the earthquake, to be sent to the Palestinian enclave. He said Israeli restrictions were leaving displaced Palestinians dependent on fabric tents, exposing them to flooding, storms and cold weather. “When floods, storms or cold weather come, they cause a disaster at least as devastating as hunger, if not more so,” he said.
articles.summary: Bureaucratic border chokeholds are weaponizing humanitarian logistics as thousands of modular container homes remain stranded at border crossings. Turkish aid shipments designed to provide emergency winter shelter remain barred by Israeli security clearance rejections. The blockade demonstrates how complete administrative control over border chokepoints can transform basic modular building materials into geopolitical bargaining chips.

articles.title: South African Rail Privatization Stumbles on Port Debt
articles.content: Durban Gateway Terminal delays continue to make headlines, but let’s turn the spotlight to another key link in the logistics chain – rail – and ask whether Transnet’s public-private model can deliver the revival it promises. By Holly Munks 22 Nov 2026 0 Shipping containers onboard a cargo ship as it departs from the Port of Durban, operated by Transnet. (Photo: Waldo Swiegers / Bloomberg via Getty Images) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper Sometimes the things that should be simplest are the most complicated. Moving goods from A to B is a great example, as the saga of Durban Gateway Terminal (DGT) reminds us.  International Container Terminal Services Inc (Ictsi), the Philippines-based company that acquired a 49% stake in DGT from Transnet, has been operating the terminal since the beginning of this year, and is in the spotlight due to a recent slowdown in cargo flows.  Read more Durban port’s crane crisis threatens SA’s private sector logistics drive November 17, 2026 An IT system update in August led to a backlog and eventual crisis serious enough to show up in earnings reports and Department of Health warnings .  “At the heart of the matter has been the poor and unsafe condition of equipment at the facility, owing to years of underinvestment and inadequate maintenance,” DGT wrote in a statement last week. Transnet begs to differ.  In a Saturday statement, the state logistics arm highlighted improvements in ship turnaround time in 2025:  “Ictsi also assumed management of Pier 2 after a significant Transnet-funded equipment-renewal programme… The broader equipment investment at Pier 2 over the preceding 18 months amounted to approximately R1.5-billion. Transnet therefore welcomes the continued investment, technology and international operating expertise being introduced by Ictsi. However, that contribution must be recognised as building on the operational recovery, equipment investment and workforce capability established before the transition, rather than starting from a position of complete operational failure.” The Southern African Association of Freight Forwarders pointed out that, from 9 to 15 November, DGT’s waterside performance was at its strongest in four months, but a recovery is not necessarily enough to handle the backlog.  At DGT, the average anchorage time was nine days, compared to zero in Cape Town and one in Ngqura and Gqeberha, over the same period. At Durban Multipurpose Terminal, not managed by Ictsi, it was 11. The average time at berth was four days at DGT and three days at Durban’s Pier 1, but only one to two days in the Eastern and Western Cape.  Break glass in case of emergency Transnet Freight Rail (TFR) is making trains available “to enable evacuation of import containers destined for Gauteng” while Transnet National Ports Authority (TNPA) has offered additional berthing capacity. Durban-bound containers are being diverted to Ngqura Container Terminal , where they “can be discharged and subsequently transferred by smaller geared vessels” to Durban.  The Port of Ngqura in Nelson Mandela Bay. (Photo: Transnet) Capacity at Durban’s Pier 1 is expected to improve with the return of ship-to-shore cranes. Transnet Port Terminals is also scouting other ports that can lend equipment, but at the moment, only Cape Town has similar equipment, and it cannot afford to give any away.  On Friday, Transnet acknowledged a list from the Department of Health of  “pharmaceutical products that were on 16 vessels in and approaching the South African port system, which required urgent evacuation”. Six ships have been unloaded, and the containers have left the port. Three will be berthed over the next few days (two at DGT), and seven are still approaching the port system. “A proposal to berth and discharge urgently needed containers at other terminals is being considered, to prevent queuing in Durban. This will be finalised before the vessels arrive,” said Transnet. On the side, TNPA has opened up the possibility of private access to Durban’s Island View precinct, a section of the harbour which handles about 74% of South Africa’s liquid bulk imports. TNPA said: “The current [expression of interest] relates exclusively to participation in existing terminal capacity and should not be construed as an invitation for the development of new petroleum storage infrastructure.” At DGT, the operators say the new software is “running smoothly”, and they are refurbishing old equipment while awaiting replacements.  By the end of the month, new empty container handlers should arrive; by the end of the first quarter of next year, second-hand straddle carriers will arrive, and by the end of Q3, shiny new straddle carriers are due. Rubber-tyred gantry cranes will arrive next December and in March 2028.  So, a bit of a wait.  DGT is also working on “a new truck appointment system”, which is where things get interesting, as we ask: what happens once the cargo actually arrives on land? Waiting on a freight train  Trade and Industrial Policy Strategies reported early this year that the proportion of SA’s total freight that moves by rail had slipped to less than 15% in 2025 from 22% in the mid-2010s.  This “contradicts the long-standing national policy goal of shifting from road to rail” – a move that would cut emissions and logistics costs, which currently represent 11.2% of gross domestic product versus 8.6% in the US.  There are many benefits to moving more cargo by rail, starting with the fact that it would make our roads much more pleasant to travel.  Moshe Motlohi, CEO of Transnet Rail Infrastructure Manager (Trim), told Daily Maverick that rail reform is not “anti-truck”, but designed to support a truck-to-train interface – letting trucks cover shorter distances and reducing driver fatigue. (Photo: Public Sector Manager / Facebook)" srcset="https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/ly9eTYCHRJsaSba9943R2eBLIrE=/450x0/smart/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 450w, https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/LR3-aSg0Ah-au7Oovvi20jIDIV8=/800x0/smart/filters:strip_exif()/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 800w, https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/taqmsUvN4Q47IFuzfoqXGch3Bm0=/1200x0/smart/filters:strip_exif()/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 1200w, https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/QN63RdhTY4gXBwe8iirufxPQyqc=/1600x0/smart/filters:strip_exif()/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 1600w, https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/IDe8mDUFLMsfYwWGsNcHWdCyd2I=/200x0/filters:strip_exif()/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 200w, https://cdn.dailymaverick.co.za/i/P7Aeb2RDGs8UlZWpJhvRnECRpvc=/400x0/filters:strip_exif()/file/attachments/orphans/Holly-freightupdate3_155518.jpg 400w" style="object-position: 50% 50%;" draggable="false" contenteditable="false"> Moshe Motlohi says rail reform is designed to support a truck-to-train interface. (Photo: Public Sector Manager / Facebook)  “We need each other,” he said. “The railway needs trucks because we cannot get door-to-door, but the trucks need us to carry more cargo, and that is going to lower the cost of doing business.” Motlohi did not specify the proportion of SA’s total cargo that Trim aims to get onto rail in 2027. He did say his team is working towards the government’s pledge of moving 250 million tonnes by rail, from 168 million at the last financial year-end.  According to Stats SA , from June to August, rail carried 43.2 million tonnes and road carried 242.8 million tonnes, meaning that for every tonne moved by rail, more than five tonnes were moved by road.  Over the last decade and a half, the share of payload transported by rail almost halved, although there has been an increase in the last year or two. (Source: Codera) SA’s railway woes are a long story. Like many former colonies, we have faced the challenge of retrofitting infrastructure designed mainly to carry natural resources off into the sunset for the benefit of others. The looting of Transnet in the State Capture era was like a sledgehammer to the knees of a struggling marathoner. One estimate puts Transnet’s State Capture debt at R60-billion. That’s billion with a “b”. Several African nations have chosen rail privatisation. Motlohi stressed that what Transnet is doing is different: it is asking companies to “co-invest”. Those who doubt the model can look to South Africa’s ports, he added. We would say, “Maybe not right now”, given the DGT debacle. Transnet’s extended cinematic universe Transnet set up Trim as a separate operating division in 2024. Trim is in charge of the actual infrastructure , allowing train operating companies (TOCs) to use the rail.  One of those TOCs is the old state entity, TFR; 11 others have secured concessions to operate on the network.  If you are confused about Transnet’s role in this, you are not alone.  A special task force was established to oversee a more definitive split of Trim from Transnet – even though Trim’s “operational and financial separation” from TFR supposedly came into effect in April last year.  The next step, according to Motlohi, is for Trim to “be corporatised out of Transnet”, but financial issues have delayed this.  Catch up Transport Minister Barbara Creecy has made the hard yards in rail reform July 9, 2026 Alistair Christison, an independent freight consultant, said the part of Transnet that is now Trim includes assets that were part of the collateral for loans previously made to Transnet.  Motlohi confirmed that “if one entity moves, it has to carry some responsibility or take an allocation of that debt.” Basically, when you try to pry Trim from Transnet, it gets messy. “Right now, Trim is not in that state of being corporatised because the financial viability is not there,” said Motlohi. Establishing Trim has brought private-sector goodwill, but Trim remains “part of Transnet… We are not privatising the ownership of the rail infrastructure,” he emphasised. Routes and regulations The government has flagged delays in corporatising Trim and establishing a transport economic regulator (TER), which it aims to have “fully operational by March 2027”. Parliament has completed the shortlist for a transport economic council, which will be part of the TER. A genuinely independent economic regulator is key to the whole system of open-access rail, Christison explained, because the regulator decides how much TOCs need to pay to use different routes.  Motlohi said Trim is not “reserving” routes for anyone (like TFR), even though some freight corridors are more profitable than others. He said the less profitable routes are still “essential” to the national economy, and Trim has requested more state funding to back them.  Transnet freight locomotives. (Photo: Guillem Sartorio / Bloomberg via Getty Images) Meanwhile, Trim has had to draft four iterations of a network statement for private partners, due to their “bankability” concerns.  Motlohi maintains that “impartiality” was built into Trim’s proposals, saying: “We don’t want anyone to feel unwelcome or that [there are] favours being done.” Ultimately, whether a private TOC invests in SA’s rail network comes down to one thing: how much money it can make. According to Christison, lack of progress is “causing most potential train operators to steer clear”.   Trim does not expect private TOCs to bear the full cost burden, hence the appeals to government.  What would really help is if someone – anyone – could do something about the route between Durban and Johannesburg, to relieve the pressure on the roads. “We are considering this corridor,” said Motlohi. It is a matter of determining how much is “fair” for the private sector to contribute.  For context Why Traxtion is sinking billions into Creecy’s freight rail reform project December 2, 2025 One company that has not steered clear is Grindrod, which ran the first test train along the North-East Corrido r earlier this month. Another two TOCs are expected to conduct test runs before the end of the year, and more next year.  “We understand that the strength of this intervention will depend on how the weakest part performs. As things stand right now, the weakest part has been either where sidings have been neglected, [or] where there’s no proper port and rail interface,” said Motlohi.  If we want to move goods around the country more easily, we all need to be on the same page and to know who is in charge – even if the structures of power involve more offshoots than a superhero franchise. articles.title: South Africa Mandates National Biometric Register for Education
articles.content: Serious gaps in employee screening across the educational system are leaving children vulnerable to risks, and to address this the Department of Basic Education needs to enforce strict compliance deadlines and provide school-by-school accountability data.   By Joy Maimela 22 Nov 2026 0 Joy Maimela is a Member of the National Assembly and Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Basic Education in Parliament. Dive Deeper Speed Read Listen Dive Deeper , which presents the writer's personal point of view. The views expressed are those of the author/authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Daily Maverick. Every parent who drops a child off at school or an early childhood development (ECD) centre entrusts the state and the adults working there with their child’s safety.  That trust carries a fundamental responsibility to ensure that everyone who has access to children is suitable to work with them. Yet, the latest figures presented to the Portfolio Committee on Basic Education reveal serious gaps in employee screening across our education system, leaving children exposed to risks that could, and must be, prevented. Vetting is not an administrative formality. It is a legal, constitutional and moral obligation. No adult who poses a risk to children should have access to them through our education system. During an oversight engagement with the departments of Basic Education , Justice and Constitutional Development, Social Development and the South African Police Service (SAPS), the committee was briefed on the extent of outstanding screening across public schools. Of approximately 458,446 educators and non-educator employees, including administrative staff, general assistants, groundskeepers and hostel employees, approximately 87% have yet to undergo the required vetting against the National Register for Sex Offenders. By 31 October 2026, provincial education departments had submitted only 159,253 applications, of which just 84,248 clearance certificates had been issued. More than 75,000 applications remained outstanding, some dating back to 2024. Most alarmingly, screening already completed identified 51 confirmed offenders working within the school system. These figures raise a disturbing question: How many more individuals who should never be working with children remain undetected because screening has not been completed? Read more How many sex offenders are there in SA’s schools? No one knows June 25, 2025 Two registers, one responsibility to protect children The committee’s engagement with the Department of Social Development highlighted why screening against the National Register for Sex Offenders alone is insufficient. The National Child Protection Register, established under Chapter 7 of the Children's Act 38 of 2005, is an equally important safeguard. These registers serve different but complementary purposes. The National Register for Sex Offenders records persons convicted of sexual offences against children and persons with mental disabilities. The National Child Protection Register comprises two parts: Part A records cases of child abuse and deliberate neglect to monitor interventions and protect affected children, while Part B records individuals found unsuitable to work with, or have access to, children. Under Section 123 of the Children’s Act, anyone whose name appears in Part B is prohibited from managing, working at or having access to children in institutions providing services to them, whether as an employee, volunteer or in another capacity. Importantly, a finding of unsuitability under Section 120 is not dependent on a criminal conviction. Courts and legally recognised disciplinary forums, including the South African Council for Educators, the Education Labour Relations Council and employers, can make such findings. This means that child-protection measures need not wait for criminal proceedings to conclude. The act requires relevant findings to be reported to the Department of Social Development within 21 working days. The SAPS also has an obligation to forward qualifying conviction information. These reporting responsibilities are critical: a register is only effective if information is submitted promptly and accurately. There is also an accountability concern regarding employer compliance. Section 126 requires those managing schools and other institutions to establish whether individuals working with, or having access to, children appear in Part B. Provincial education departments have had access to the register since 2022/23. The Department of Basic Education and provinces must therefore account for how effectively they have used this system and how many employees have actually been screened. Having access to the register is not the same as complying with the law. No loopholes in ECD centres and independent schools Child protection cannot end at public school gates. Children attending ECD centres and independent schools are equally entitled to protection. Younger children are particularly vulnerable because they may lack the language or ability to disclose abuse. The departments of Basic Education and Social Development must ensure that screening obligations extend across public schools, independent schools, ECD facilities and contracted services involving access to children. No individual found unsuitable should be able to move between institutions because of fragmented screening systems or employers failing to conduct the required checks. Recent cases include allegations of the rape of a nine-year-old learner by an educator in Soweto, and a case at Mbambangalo High School near Pietermaritzburg where a 41-year-old teacher was arrested and placed on leave following allegations of sexual abuse involving learners.  The provincial Department of Education confirmed that two cases had been reported to the district, while LifeLine Pietermaritzburg reported receiving complaints involving 11 learners. This demonstrates the devastating consequences of abuse by adults in positions of authority. Schools must report allegations, protect victims and refer suspected criminal conduct to the relevant authorities. Abuse must never be concealed through informal agreements or internal processes intended to protect institutional reputations. Read more Teacher vetting crisis: over 81% of educators remain unchecked amidst child safety concerns May 14, 2025 Accountability before the March 2027 deadline The Department of Social Development has confirmed that Part B is maintained electronically and updated as new information is received. It has also committed to assisting the Department of Basic Education with bulk suitability verification as an interim measure while longer-term digital integration is developed. This commitment must translate into measurable progress. The 31 March 2027 deadline arises from a court-ordered settlement following litigation by the Teddy Bear Foundation, represented by SECTION27, to strengthen implementation of the National Child Protection Register. The Department of Basic Education and provincial departments must complete the vetting of existing employees against Part B by this date.  With approximately 458,446 employees requiring screening, the slow progress is deeply concerning. Departments must urgently accelerate verification, address administrative bottlenecks and demonstrate how they will meet this binding deadline. The Department of Justice and Constitutional Development, the Department of Social Development and SAPS must also fulfil their respective screening, information-sharing and processing responsibilities. The South African Council for Educators and other disciplinary structures must ensure that findings of unsuitability are reported promptly. The committee expects accurate records, regular progress reports and clear accountability for missed targets. New appointments must also undergo the necessary checks before individuals are permitted to work with children. The committee will continue to exercise rigorous oversight over every department and institution responsible for fulfilling these obligations. Administrative inefficiency, fragmented databases and poor coordination cannot remain excuses for exposing children to preventable harm. Our responsibility is not simply to ensure that schools are staffed, but to ensure that they are safe. Every child has a constitutional right to protection from maltreatment, neglect, abuse and degradation. That right cannot be compromised by bureaucratic delays or institutional failures. Protecting our children is non-negotiable. Every adult working with them must be vetted, every finding of unsuitability must be acted upon and every department must be held accountable for keeping our children safe. DM Joy Maimela is a Member of the National Assembly and Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Basic Education in Parliament.
